analysis.one_liner: Directs the Treasury to list and break up banks too big to fail.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee with only its sponsor and one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Within 90 days, the Treasury Secretary would have had to name every commercial bank, investment bank, hedge fund, and insurance company whose failure would wreck the economy without a taxpayer bailout. Starting one year later, the Secretary would have had to break those companies up so none of them could hold the economy hostage again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and depositors, who after the 2008 crisis had seen their money used to rescue giant financial firms. Smaller banks and credit unions would also benefit from competition on a level field, since today's largest firms effectively carry an implicit government guarantee that lets them borrow more cheaply.

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the Treasury Secretary to compile and publish a list of every financial entity considered too big to fail, ending the practice where officials decide case by case which firms get rescued.

Beginning one year after enactment, the Treasury would have had to break up those firms so that none could fail in a way that would cause a catastrophic effect on the U.S. or global economy without a taxpayer bailout.
The bill defined the problem explicitly: any entity so large that its failure would destabilize the financial system or economy without substantial government assistance.

analysis.who_pays: The largest commercial banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies, whose shareholders would absorb the cost of splitting into smaller companies and would lose the implicit taxpayer guarantee that lowers their borrowing costs and shields them from failure.

drawbacks.text: The bill gave the Treasury Secretary sweeping, one-way power: he alone would decide who goes on the list and then alone would direct the breakups, with no stated criteria, hearings, or judicial review in the bill text.

Forcing rapid divestiture of systemically large firms within a single year could have disrupted credit markets and customers while assets were sold off, a risk that even many financial-reform advocates preferred to address through resolution regimes and capital rules rather than mandated breakups.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — that no private company should be so large that taxpayers must rescue it — addresses a real cost ordinary people bore in 2008. But the bill was a two-page directive with almost no machinery: no size thresholds, no process, no oversight of how the breakups would happen, and one official handed unilateral power to restructure major companies. The idea had broad public resonance; this particular vehicle was a statement bill, not workable legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the Too Big to Fail, Too Big to Exist Act on November 19, 2009.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee that handles banking legislation.
One other House member, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies kept their size and the implicit taxpayer backstop that comes with being too big to fail. Had the bill become law, those firms would have been required to break up.

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Treasury to list and break up too-big-to-fail firms.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats touched the bill — the sponsor and a single cosponsor — and no Republican supported it, so the outcome reflects near-total absence of support in both parties rather than a partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced the biggest banks to break up, costing shareholders and management their scale. Their gain from the bill dying is keeping the implicit federal guarantee that makes them safer bets for creditors and lets them borrow more cheaply than smaller rivals — a subsidy ordinary taxpayers stand behind.
Funds deemed too big to fail would have been on the Treasury's list and subject to breakup, ending the implicit rescue expectation their largest players enjoy.
Systemically large insurers (the 2008 rescue of AIG being the model) would have been listed and broken up rather than bailed out next time.
